sections.text: When a man renounces even the thought of initiating action, when he is not interested in sense objects or any results which may flow from his acts, then in truth he understands spirituality.
Let him seek liberation by the help of his Highest Self, and let him never disgrace his own Self. For that Self is his only friend; yet it may also be his enemy.
To him who has conquered his lower nature by Its help, the Self is a friend, but to him who has not done so, It is an enemy.

What is my purpose and destiny? We have been discussing Chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, Yoga of Contemplation and Meditation. In the first five chapters, we have seen that Bhagavan defined the word Yoga. In chapter two, Bhagavan defined Yoga: Samatvam Yoga Uchyate -- Yoga is the balance of mind.
And then he said, Yogah karmasu kaushalam -- Yoga is dexterity in action. That was given as the goal. Yoga is to balance your mind. Your mind should be balanced in all situations, and thats your goal.
Then the next three chapters -- 3, 4, and 5 -- give two techniques to achieve that yoga of balancing the mind. The first is Karma Yoga: do not depend on the Karma Phala. Giving up expectations for results is the technique we call Karma Yoga.
The other technique is giving up the sense of agency, which is called sannyasa. These two techniques represent two different modes. One promotes actions, but without any expectation of the fruits.
The other promotes inaction -- giving up the sense of agency is giving up actions. I am not doing anything. So for an average person, it may seem contradictory. One promotes actions, the other promotes inaction. Also, culturally we have seen that a Karma Yogi is engaged in actions, while a sannyasi has given up all actions.
He gives up his job, he gives up his family. Even in olden days, a grihastha was required to perform certain rituals daily. As we have seen, he keeps fire burning in his house all the time because he needs it for performing the rituals.
But once he becomes a sannyasi, he is not required to perform any of those actions. So in the narrow sense, the Karma Kanda says that a grihastha is required to perform ritualistic actions and a sannyasi is not. We have seen these two opposite sides of the same coin, seemingly contrary to each other.
That can create confusion in our mind: is the tyagi or yogi better, or is the sannyasi better? Therefore the chapter opened with a clear declaration from Bhagavan: Anashritah karmaphalam karyam karma karoti yah -- sa sannyasi cha yogi cha. Bhagavan once again extols Karma Yoga as the very means of achieving this balance of mind. One who performs actions without depending on the fruits of action is both a yogi and a sannyasi, because sannyasa cannot be achieved -- nor can yoga be achieved -- by merely renouncing actions.
Both achieve the same goal of samatvam, the balance of mind which we are looking for. Therefore: Yam sannyasam iti prahuh yogam tam viddhi Pandava -- know that sannyasa is the same thing as what they call Yoga. One who has not given up Sankalpa cannot become a yogi.
But depending on your progress in the evolutionary process of reaching from the lower to the higher, you can choose one or the other. So in the third verse we have seen: Arurukshoh muner yogam karma karanam uchyate. If youre still not there, if youre not established in Yoga, then Karma is the means.
If I cant balance my mind, I know that I can lose balance when a situation occurs which is not conducive. When things are going well, I act very rationally. Its only when things are not going right that I become irrational.
The irrationality, Bhagavan says, shows that you have no control over your mind. The situation is affecting you, and you blame the situation. But the root cause is that you have no control over your mind.
The mind is taking away the peace in your inner self. Therefore Bhagavan says, keep doing actions without expectations. Thats your exercise.
Continue working on that. Yogarudhasya tasyaiva shamah karanam uchyate -- but one who has balanced his mind, one who has achieved the state of yoga, for him shamah (quiescence of mind) is the means. The mind has no desire, no thoughts of achieving something.
He doesnt become thoughtless, but he does not have any goal of achieving something he does not have, because he feels complete. All our plans for achieving things are because we feel incomplete. Without my car, Im incomplete.
So the things that make me feel incomplete, I try to acquire from the outside world. When you feel incomplete and you have to get something out of this world -- thats the power of Sankalpa. In your mind you create a situation.
You really create a scenario that if I have this then I will feel complete. If I come here on any kind of student visa or H1 visa only if I can get green card then everything will be solved. Once I get green card, things will be perfectly fine.
That becomes a Sankalpa, an overarching desire. Now, who is considered to be Yogarudha? One who has balanced his mind, who now has control over his mind. Here is the litmus test: not getting attached to sense objects does not mean I do not use sense objects.
But I use them for utility. I feel thirsty and I drink water. I feel hungry and I eat food.
But I dont get attached to them. And I have to have this amras every day. Thats an attachment.
Enjoying mango juice is not a problem. Getting attached to the taste is the problem. So Bhagavan said, one who doesnt get attached to sense objects -- he uses them for whatever utility they provide for maintaining his life, but doesnt get attached to them.
If they are not there tomorrow, he will still be the same person. This part is even more difficult. We can probably get detached from sense objects, but getting detached from my own actions is harder.
Therefore we have discussed many times before: retiring is not that easy. Giving up something which Ive been doing all my life is difficult. I know it very well because Im not retired yet.
Its very difficult to give up actions which you are performing and getting used to them. Those actions define myself. The first thing that comes out of your mouth: Im an architect -- because that defines who you are.
Thats your profession. Oh, Im a son of such and such. Well, thats your relationship. We continue this inquiry of defining ourselves, and we miserably fail in the end, because everything we use to define ourselves is some kind of relationship, some acquisition, some position -- but not really who you are. That Bhagavan says is attachment to your actions.
You call yourself an architect because youre attached to your profession. You call yourself a father because youre attached to your relationship with your. Those attachments are to my actions, not to the sense objects.
Im not attached to my son. Im attached to my actions, my profession. Thats attachment to action.
But someone who has given up that attachment -- that does not mean he does not have relationships or doesnt work. He considers that as part of this world where he has to function. Sarvasankalpa Sannyasi.
These words come time and again, and therefore we obviously have to understand them as thoroughly as we can. The word Sankalpa comes in our culture all the time. As we discussed last time, when you go to do puja, Panditji will ask you to make Sankalpa -- this puja, Im doing it for such and such. The Sankalpa is Samyak Kalpana.
The word samyak literally means overarching, encompassing everything. That is Samyak Kalpana. When there is an overarching desire in my mind -- I want to get this -- thats Sankalpa.
It is a firm determination that my happiness lies there and I must get it. So Panditji says, when you are doing a puja, you must do Sankalpa, Samyak Kalpana: By doing this puja, I shall get this. Our mind does that Sankalpa all the time. The only problem is it continues to change.
Bhagavan said this mind has the capacity to jump from one Sankalpa to another, and that creates a variety of desires. In the Mahabharata, theres a statement which says: Kamah, janami te mulam -- O desire, I know your roots. Your roots are Sankalpa.
I know that you are born out of Sankalpa, the desire which is defining me. The Upanishad also says the self is nothing but the identification with desire which I consider to be me. The Mahabharata says: O desire, you are born from Sankalpa.
Therefore I will never think about you, and you will be destroyed along with your own roots. If I dont have Sankalpa, I dont give rise to desire. Then there wont be any desire. And I can kill the desire.
Sarva Sankalpa sanyasi. Therefore, the word Sarva Sankalpa is constantly changing. We constantly change our overarching desire.
Today this is what I want to achieve, and then tomorrow it changes. Unless we curb that urge to create new Sankalpas, I cannot become a sannyasi. So he said, Sarva Sankalpa Sannyasi -- one who has given up all Sankalpas.
Yogarudha ta duchyate -- that person is considered established in Yoga. If I feel complete, I will not have a desire to achieve anything overarchingly. I will have needs and Ill fulfill my needs.
I need water because Im thirsty. I need food because Im hungry. I need a job because I need to make a living.
Those are normal things we do. But when there is a Sankalpa -- this is what I need to get so that I feel happy -- Bhagavan says that one who gives up that sense of Sankalpa becomes Yogarudha. If you find yourself in that situation where you have no desire to achieve anything, Bhagavan said you are Yogarudha at that point.
Shamah karanam uchyate -- for such a person, inactivity is the means. In fact, from the scriptural point of view, the time comes when you have to stop your activity. It is a sin not to act when you are required to act, but it is also equally dangerous if you continue acting when youre not required to act.
And therefore we used to have those ashrams: Brahmacharyashram, Grihasthashram, Vanaprasthashram, Sannyasashram. You have to reach a point in your life where inactivity is your goal, and then start working not for the self but on the self. Uddharet atmanatmanam na atmanam avasadayet.
It seems like there are two me. One is the watching me and one is the working me. The watching me is constantly deciding what needs to be done. It is what we call our own conscience -- we feel this is right. But then my pragmatic thought says, No, that may not be very useful, so lets go and do that instead. This watching me is my higher self.
Consider that which has a clear vision of what is right and what is wrong, constantly watching me. I think I should have a cup of tea. There are two Is -- one who thinks, one who wants the cup of tea. This watching me is the one who can guide you. And Bhagavan said, Uddharet atmanatmanam -- let your lower self -- the working me -- be raised out of this sansar, this jagat which is constantly changing.
Raise that lower, working self by the help of the watching self. Then my own conscience can help me get out of the sorrows of day-to-day life, if I become friends with it, if I listen to that voice. Na atmanam avasadayet -- dont let this working me drown in this world of sorrows and day-to-day rut.
Atmaiva hi atmano bandhuh -- that watching me can be my friend, if I allow it to be my friend.

Uddhared atmanatmanam - lift yourself by your own self. This powerful instruction from verse 5 reveals that within you exists both the problem and the solution. There is a working self caught in day-to-day struggles, and a watching self that observes with clarity and wisdom. That inner voice of conscience, so often drowned out by the noise of desires and fears, is your higher self ready to guide you upward. The question is: which self are you listening to?
The teaching about the self being both friend and enemy is startlingly practical. When you have mastery over your senses and mind, the same higher self that could drag you into deeper confusion becomes your greatest ally, empowering every positive step. But when you lose control - when I want that coffee right now overrides your better judgment - that same powerful self enables your downfall. It is like the fuel in a car: in a controlled vehicle, it takes you where you want to go; in an out-of-control vehicle, it powers the crash.
Today, practice noticing the two selves in operation. When a strong desire arises - for food, for approval, for a purchase - pause and observe. Is this the restless lower self demanding satisfaction, or a genuine need? Then consciously invoke the watching self: What would my wisest self advise here? This simple practice of self-observation, done repeatedly throughout the day, is the beginning of making the higher self your friend.
